quests.question: He promised he ___ the report before the deadline.
quests.hint: 'Will' in direct speech shifts to 'would' in reported speech.
quests.explanation: In reported speech, 'will' shifts to 'would': I will submit the report → He promised he would submit the report. 'Would submit' (not 'would have submitted', which implies it is already done).

quests.question: She warned us ___ touch the equipment.
quests.hint: Reported negative commands: 'warned us ___ touch'.
quests.explanation: Reported negative commands/warnings use 'not to + infinitive': She warned us not to touch the equipment. Positive: She told us to be careful. Pattern: tell/warn/advise/ask + object + not to + base verb.

quests.question: They denied ___ responsible for the incident.
quests.hint: 'Deny' is followed by a gerund.
quests.explanation: 'Deny + gerund': They denied being responsible. 'Deny doing something' = say you did not do it. Also: deny making, deny having. 'Deny + that clause' also works: They denied that they were responsible.

quests.question: ___ student must submit the assignment by Friday.
quests.hint: Which quantifier uses a singular noun and singular verb?
quests.explanation: 'Every + singular noun + singular verb': Every student must submit. 'All + plural noun': All students must submit. 'Each' also uses singular: Each student must submit. 'Both' implies exactly two.

quests.question: I like ___ options - either would work for me.
quests.hint: Two options are acceptable - which means 'the two'?
quests.explanation: 'Both' refers to two things and means 'the two': I like both options. 'Either' = one or the other. 'Neither' = not one or the other (negative). 'Each' focuses on items individually.

quests.question: ___ of the candidates was particularly impressive.
quests.hint: Two candidates were not impressive - which negative word fits?
quests.explanation: 'Neither' is negative and refers to exactly two: Neither of the candidates was impressive = not the first and not the second. 'None' is used for three or more: None of the five candidates was impressive.

quests.question: He worked overtime ___ to his regular duties.
quests.hint: Which phrase adds information to what already exists?
quests.explanation: 'In addition to' and 'as well as' both add information: He worked overtime in addition to/as well as his regular duties. 'In addition' (without 'to') connects sentences: He worked overtime. In addition, he attended all meetings.

quests.question: Success came ___ her personal life.
quests.hint: Her success harmed her personal life - which phrase shows this trade-off?
quests.explanation: 'At the expense of' = by sacrificing or harming something else: Success came at the expense of her personal life. This phrase implies a cost or negative consequence of achieving something.

quests.question: She completed the course ___ all the difficulties she faced.
quests.hint: Which concession word is followed by a noun phrase?
quests.explanation: 'Despite + noun/noun phrase/gerund': despite all the difficulties. 'In spite of' works the same way. 'Although' and 'even though' need a subject + verb clause: although she faced difficulties.

quests.question: The company showed great ___ in responding to the crisis.
quests.hint: After 'great', we need a noun form.
quests.explanation: After adjectives like 'great', 'complete', 'significant', we need a noun. Flexible → flexibility (-ity suffix). Other examples: able → ability, creative → creativity, sensitive → sensitivity.

quests.question: The results were quite ___.
quests.hint: The results were surprising - choose the correct adjective form.
quests.explanation: 'Unexpected' = not expected, surprising. The prefix 'un-' adds a negative meaning: expected → unexpected, usual → unusual, reliable → unreliable. 'Unexpectedly' is an adverb - wrong in this position.

quests.question: She has ___ ability to connect with people.
quests.hint: Before a noun (ability), we need an adjective with an article.
quests.explanation: 'A remarkable ability': remarkable (adjective) + ability (noun). Note: 'remarkable' starts with a consonant sound, so use 'a', not 'an'. 'Remarkably' is an adverb: remarkably fast. Check the word class needed.

quests.question: I ___ this problem all morning and I still haven't solved it.
quests.hint: The activity started this morning and is still ongoing.
quests.explanation: Present perfect continuous (have been + -ing): used for activities in progress from a past time up to now, emphasising duration: I have been thinking about this all morning. Still unresolved.

quests.question: When I arrived, they ___ a heated debate.
quests.hint: An ongoing action at a specific past moment.
quests.explanation: Past continuous (were having) = an action in progress at a specific past moment: When I arrived (past moment), they were having a debate (in progress). Past perfect continuous would imply the debate had ended before I arrived.

quests.question: By the time you read this, I ___ the country.
quests.hint: A completed future action before another future point.
quests.explanation: Future perfect (will have + past participle): I will have left the country = the leaving will be completed before you read this. Future perfect shows completion before a future reference point.

quests.question: The project took twice ___ long as expected.
quests.hint: Multiplication in comparison: 'twice as ___ as'.
quests.explanation: 'Twice as long as' is a comparison using a multiplier: twice as long as expected. Structure: X times + as + adjective + as. Examples: three times as expensive as, half as much as, four times as fast as.

quests.question: The ___ you practise, the better you get.
quests.hint: Double comparatives express a proportional relationship.
quests.explanation: 'The more..., the better' is a double comparative: The more you practise, the better you get. It shows that as one thing increases, another also changes. The + comparative, the + comparative.

quests.question: She earns ___ less than her male colleagues.
quests.hint: Which word can intensify a comparative adjective?
quests.explanation: 'Far' (and 'much', 'a lot', 'considerably', 'significantly') can intensify comparative forms: far less, much better, considerably larger. Never use 'very' before comparatives - 'very better' is incorrect.

quests.question: The government had to ___ the plan due to public opposition.
quests.hint: The plan was cancelled - which phrasal verb means 'to cancel'?
quests.explanation: 'Call off' = to cancel: They had to call off the plan. 'Put off' = to postpone (delay to a later time). 'Give up on' = to stop trying. 'Back out' = to withdraw from an agreement. Each has a distinct meaning.

quests.question: She couldn't ___ the idea of selling her childhood home.
quests.hint: She found it emotionally difficult to accept.
quests.explanation: 'Come to terms with' = to accept or deal with something difficult: She couldn't come to terms with selling her home. 'Put up with' = tolerate. 'Get away with' = escape consequences. 'Look into' = investigate.

quests.question: The detective decided to ___ the case more carefully.
quests.hint: The detective is going to investigate further.
quests.explanation: 'Look into' = to investigate or examine: look into the case. 'Look up' = search for information. 'Look over' = review quickly. 'Look after' = take care of. Phrasal verbs have meanings distinct from their parts.

quests.question: ___ in Paris, she speaks French fluently.
quests.hint: The passive meaning of 'being born' in the past requires which form?
quests.explanation: 'Having been born' is the perfect passive participle: Having been born in Paris, she speaks French fluently. It shows the first action is completed and occurred before the main clause. 'Born' alone also works informally.

quests.question: Not ___ what to say, she remained silent.
quests.hint: Present participle for a simultaneous situation.
quests.explanation: 'Not knowing what to say' = because she didn't know what to say. Present participle clauses (not knowing, feeling, seeing) express a situation simultaneous with or causing the action of the main clause.

quests.question: The book ___, she returned it to the library.
quests.hint: An absolute participle clause - the book is the subject of 'finished'.
quests.explanation: 'The book finished' is an absolute participle clause (with its own subject, different from the main clause subject). 'Having finished the book, she returned it' is another valid form where the subject is the same throughout.

quests.question: ___ you need any help, please don't hesitate to ask.
quests.hint: Formal first conditional - 'if' replaced by inversion.
quests.explanation: 'Should + subject + base verb' = 'If + subject + should + base verb' in formal English: Should you need any help = If you should need any help. This inversion is common in formal letters and official notices.

quests.question: ___ I in your position, I would reconsider.
quests.hint: Second conditional inversion - 'were' moves to the front.
quests.explanation: 'Were + subject...' = 'If + subject + were...' in formal English: Were I in your position = If I were in your position. This inversion replaces 'if' and is formal or literary in style.

quests.question: ___ she told me the truth, I would have forgiven her.
quests.hint: Third conditional inversion - which auxiliary moves to the front?
quests.explanation: 'Had + subject + past participle' = 'If + subject + had + past participle' (third conditional inversion): Had she told me the truth = If she had told me the truth. Had, were, and should can all replace 'if' in formal conditionals.

quests.question: The meeting ___ at that time.
quests.hint: An ongoing action at a past moment, described passively.
quests.explanation: Past continuous passive: was/were + being + past participle: The meeting was still being held at that time. This combines the continuity of past continuous with passive voice.

quests.question: The contract ___ by both parties before the deadline.
quests.hint: The signing was completed before another past event (the deadline).
quests.explanation: Past perfect passive: had been + past participle: The contract had been signed before the deadline. Shows a passive action completed before another past reference point.

quests.question: The new product ___ next spring.
quests.hint: The product is the thing being launched - passive is needed.
quests.explanation: Future passive: will be + past participle: The new product will be launched next spring. The focus is on the product, not who launches it. 'Will launch' would wrongly make the product the one doing the launching.
